sub_strands.sub_strand: Polite Language: Telephone Etiquette (Theme 1: Human rights)
learning_experiences: listen and identify words and phrases that indicate polite language in a telephone conversation from a digital device,
role-play a telephone dialogue on human rights using polite language,
match polite telephone conversation expressions with appropriate responses from the cards provided,
practise leaving and taking telephone messages over the phone using polite language on a caller card.
key_inquiry_questions: Why should one be polite when speaking over telephone?
How do we ensure politeness in a telephone conversation?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Communication: It is enhanced as the learner speaks with clarity while carrying out telephone conversations.
Digital literacy: It is enhanced as the learner uses the telephone to make calls under the guidance of the teacher.
sub_strands.values: Respect: It is inculcated as the learner appreciates diverse opinions while taking turns during telephone conversations.
sub_strands.pcis: Social cohesion: This is developed as the learner uses polite language when communicating over the phone.
sub_strands.links: Use of polite language is taught in other languages like Kiswahili and it is also emphasized in Religious Education.

outcomes.text: identify polite words and phrases in telephone conversations
conduct a telephone conversation using polite words and expressions
acknowledge the significance of etiquette in telephone conversations

sub_strands.sub_strand: Extensive Reading: Independent Reading (Theme 1: Human rights)
learning_experiences: skim through grade-appropriate print and electronic reading materials,
scan grade-appropriate print and electronic reading materials,
read materials on human rights at their pace within a specified period,
discuss what they have read,
write down the main ideas in the texts they have read,
use a dictionary to look up the meaning of vocabulary acquired from independent reading,
infer the meaning of words as used in the texts.
key_inquiry_questions: Why should one read widely?
What should one consider when selecting a reading text?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Self–efficacy: This is enhanced when the learner improves their self-esteem as they choose the texts to read.
Learning to learn: It is enhanced as the learner gains assertiveness and independence when they select reading materials.
sub_strands.values: Responsibility: It is developed as the learner engages and helps peers in selecting reading materials.
sub_strands.pcis: Decision-making: This is improved as the learner chooses what to read extensively from a variety of materials.
sub_strands.links: The learner relates the concept of human rights to the study of other learning areas such as Social Studies which handles human rights as a pertinent issue.

outcomes.text: identify print and non-print texts that are interesting to read
read a range of texts for information
appreciate the importance of reading for enjoyment

sub_strands.sub_strand: Word classes: Compound Nouns (Theme 1: Human rights)
learning_experiences: listen to an audio recording on human rights,
identify the compound nouns used in the text,
work with peers to categorise compound nouns into two-word or three-word nouns from a given list,
form separate and hyphenated compound nouns by combining two or more words,
form plurals of compound nouns from a completion table,
write sentences using compound nouns in their singular and plural forms,
search online and offline for more examples of compound nouns,
use compound nouns to form sentences from a substitution table,
assess the correctness of the sentences with peers.
key_inquiry_questions: Why should we use compound nouns when communicating?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Communication and collaboration: It is enhanced as the learner work with peers categorise compound nouns
Self-efficacy: It is enhanced as the learner shows concerted attention to detail when forming separate and hyphenated compound nouns by combining two or more words.
Learning to learn: It is enhanced as the learner engages in self- driven tasks while using compound nouns in sentences.
sub_strands.values: Respect: It is promoted as the learner displays patience while working with peers to identify the compound nouns in the text.
sub_strands.pcis: Effective communication: It is boosted as the learner communicates using the newly acquired compound nouns.
sub_strands.links: The learner is able to relate the use of compound nouns in learning similar concept in other languages such as Kiswahili.

outcomes.text: identify compound nouns in a text
use compound nouns in their singular and plural forms
appreciate the importance of compound nouns in communication

skills.name: Tell compound nouns and write their singular and plural forms
skills.mastery: Recognises a compound noun (toothbrush, post office, mother-in-law), writes its plural by changing the main word (post offices, mothers-in-law, toothbrushes), and does not write the plural on the last part only (mother-in-laws), in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 7 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Grade 7 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Puts the plural -s on the last part of a hyphenated compound (mother-in-laws, passer-bys).

example.question: My two ___ came to the party.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "mother-in-laws" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The main noun takes the plural: mothers, then in-law.
misconceptions.feedback: In a hyphenated compound the main noun takes the plural: mothers-in-law, passers-by, not mother-in-laws.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes a one-word compound as two words (tooth brush, class room) or the other way round.

example.question: Wanjiru bought a new ___.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "tooth brush" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Check the dictionary: some compounds are one word, some two.
misconceptions.feedback: Some compound nouns are one word (toothbrush, classroom), some are two (post office), and some have a hyphen (mother-in-law). Look in a dictionary.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Leaves a compound noun singular where a plural is needed.

example.question: The ___ sell stamps.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "post office" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Ask: one or many? Many needs the plural -s on the main noun.
misconceptions.feedback: Many post offices sell stamps. Put the plural on the main noun.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

learning_experiences: predict events by focusing on the title and illustrations in a text,
silently read the short story,
infer contextual meanings of words based on the events in the story,
retell the story while citing issues on human rights,
role-play selected events and characters in the story,
work with peers to discuss the relationships between their own lives and those of characters in the text.
key_inquiry_questions: How can you predict the outcome of a story even before you read it?
How do you tell the meaning of unfamiliar words in a story?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Critical thinking: It is promoted as the learner assesses the relationship between their own lives and those of the characters in the story.
Citizenship: It is promoted as the learner cites issues on human rights.
sub_strands.values: Responsibility: It is promoted as the learner takes different roles to dramatise the events in the story.
sub_strands.pcis: Environmental and social issues: It is promoted as the learner compares their experiences with those of the characters in the story.
sub_strands.links: Intensive reading is handled in Kiswahili.

outcomes.text: outline the sequence of events in a short story that they have read
use contextual clues to infer the meanings of words
answer direct and inferential questions from a short story
acknowledge the role of reading in communication

copy a provided passage and space letters, words and sentences correctly,
rewrite a provided text legibly and neatly,
cancel words or sentences neatly when composing a text,
split words that are joined appropriately,
write dictated sentences legibly and neatly,
write a narrative composition on human rights legibly and neatly,
cancel neatly upon making mistakes as they listen to the excerpt that is dictated.

What are the qualities of a good handwriting?

Learning to learn: It is enhanced as the learner completes tasks on time as he or she writes texts legibly and neatly.
Self-efficacy: It is enhanced as the learner’s confidence in written communication is boosted.
sub_strands.values: Responsibility: This is enhanced as the learner legibly and neatly writes words and sentences related to human rights.
sub_strands.pcis: Effective communication: It is improved as the learner practises writing legibly and neatly.
sub_strands.links: The learner is able to apply the skill of writing neatly and legibly while writing essays in Religious Education.

outcomes.text: classify letters according to height differentials
write a text, legibly and neatly
advocate the need for legibility and neatness in writing

sub_strands.links: The learner is able to apply the skills acquired in drama performance techniques to Creative arts and sports.

use performance techniques when singing

sub_strands.values: Responsibility: It is enhanced as the learner engages in writing poems on scientific innovations in groups.
sub_strands.pcis: Social cohesion is developed as the learner works together with peers to compose poems on scientific innovations.
sub_strands.links: The learner is able to relate to concepts learnt in poetry to their learning in Kiswahili.

learning_experiences: list the collective nouns as they listen to an audio text,
identify collective nouns in a print text,
classify collective nouns according to people, animals or things,
discuss the plural forms of these nouns,
write correct sentences using collective nouns from substitution tables,
fill in blank spaces using the correct collective nouns,
fill in crossword puzzles using collective nouns,
search for more examples of collective nouns from print or non-print text,

key_inquiry_questions: How do collective nouns form their plurals?

Unity: It is developed as the learner collaborates with peers to construct sentences using the collective nouns they have identified.

use singular and plural forms of collective nouns correctly in sentences

skills.name: Use collective nouns correctly
skills.mastery: Picks the collective noun that fits a group (a pride of lions, a fleet of ships, a school of fish, a troop of monkeys, a crew of sailors) and writes it as one singular word (a flock, not a flocks) before of, and does not use one group word for every group, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 7 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Grade 7 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Uses the wrong collective noun for a group (a herd of fish, a swarm of lions).

example.question: A ___ of lions rested under the tree.

misconceptions.cause: Uses one word for every group.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "swarm" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Each group has its own word.
misconceptions.feedback: Each kind of group has its own collective noun: a pride of lions, a school of fish, a fleet of ships, a troop of monkeys, a crew of sailors.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes the collective noun as a plural (a flocks of birds, a crews of sailors).

example.question: A ___ of sailors boarded the ship.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "crews" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: One group is one thing, so one crew.
misconceptions.feedback: A collective noun names one group, so write a crew of sailors, not a crews of sailors.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Leaves out of after the collective noun (a swarm bees).

example.question: A swarm ___ bees settled on the roof.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "for" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The words go: a swarm of bees.
misconceptions.feedback: Say a swarm of bees. The collective noun is followed by of.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Intensive Reading: Short story (Class Reader) (Theme 2: Scientific innovations)
learning_experiences: watch different places and times of the day and night from a digital device or written text,
read a short story and retell what they have read,
tease out the geographical setting, the historical period and the culture from which the story is based by looking at the words and elements used in the story,
work with peers to compare the setting and places in the short story to their own real life setting,
use their surroundings to describe the setting and place,
draw or take pictures of different settings at different times.
key_inquiry_questions: Which places in the short stories would you like to visit?
Which time in history would you desire to live?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Digital literacy: It is enhanced as the learner manipulates digital devices while looking at different places at different times.
Imagination and creativity: These are brought out as the learner undertakes tasks that encourage artistic expression while drawing or taking pictures of different settings.
sub_strands.values: Unity: It is fostered as the learner displays team spirit while working with peers to compare the setting in the short story with that of their environment.
sub_strands.pcis: Peace education: It is enhanced as the learner appreciates the fact that different people live in different places.
sub_strands.links: The learner is able to relate the content of short stories to similar content in other subjects such as Religious Education.

outcomes.text: identify the setting - time and place-of a short story
highlight the episodes in the short story chronologically
appreciate the differences in culture and setting

sub_strands.sub_strand: Mechanics of Writing: Punctuation (Theme 2: Scientific innovations)
learning_experiences: search online and offline on uses of the comma, apostrophe and capital letter,
read a given text and take note of the commas, apostrophes and capital letters used,
explain how the commas and the apostrophes are used in the text,
discuss the role of capital letters as used in various words or sentences in the passage,
punctuate a passage correctly using commas, apostrophes, or capital letters where necessary,
write a short composition on scientific innovations using capital letters, commas and apostrophes correctly,
assess each other’s composition and discuss how the punctuation marks and capital letters have been used,
search for more uses of the apostrophe and brackets from books or the internet.
key_inquiry_questions: Why should a text be well punctuated?
How does wrong punctation affect writing?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Self-efficacy:It is developed as the learner gains confidence to use punctuation marks correctly in speech and in writing.
Critical thinking and problem solving: It is enhanced as the learner figures out when to use a comma, appostrophe and capital letter.
sub_strands.values: Respect: It is inculcated as the learner assesses peers’ work while tolerating any errors of punctuation.
sub_strands.pcis: Decision making skills: They are enhanced as the learner decides on what and where to punctuate correctly in writing.
sub_strands.links: The learner relates correct use of commas, apostrophes and capital letters in written work in subjects such as Agriculture .

outcomes.text: punctuate a given text using commas, apostrophes, and capital letters correctly
use an apostrophe, commas and capital letters appropriately in composition writing
advocate the use of correct punctuation in writing

skills.name: Use commas, apostrophes and capital letters correctly
skills.mastery: Puts commas between the items of a list and after an opening word, writes the apostrophe for belonging (the boy's book, the boys' books) and for a short form (it's, don't) but not for a plain plural, and writes capital letters for names, the first word and I, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 7 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Grade 7 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Puts an apostrophe in a plain plural (apple's for sale, the boy's are here).

example.question: Mama bought three ___ at the market.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "mango's" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A plain plural does not take an apostrophe.
misconceptions.feedback: An apostrophe shows belonging or a short form, not a plural: three mangoes, not three mango's.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Puts the apostrophe in the wrong place for belonging (the boys book, the boy's books for many boys).

example.question: The ___ bags are in the classroom. (many boys)

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "boy's" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: One owner: 's. Many owners ending in s: s'.
misconceptions.feedback: For one owner write the boy's bag. For many owners write the boys' bags, with the apostrophe after the s.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Leaves out the commas in a list or puts one before the last item wrongly.

example.question: We bought rice___ beans and maize.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Separate the items in a list with commas.
misconceptions.feedback: Put a comma between the items of a list and use and before the last: rice, beans and maize.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Mixes its and it's.

example.question: The cow licked ___ calf.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "it's" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: It's means it is. Its shows belonging.
misconceptions.feedback: Its (no apostrophe) shows belonging: its calf. It's is short for it is or it has.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

respond to oral questions based on the text correctly,
identify and write down the ideas presented in the text,
orally answer questions based on the text,
make a list of unfamiliar words and practise pronouncing them,
give the meaning of specific words using context clues,
look up the meanings of unfamiliar words from an online or offline dictionary,
use given words to construct sentences.
key_inquiry_questions: What should one look for when listening to a text?

sub_strands.values: Responsibility: It is cultivated as the learner acquires knowledge about how to take care of the environment from the cause and effect text on pollution.
sub_strands.pcis: Environmental education awareness: It is enhanced as the learner listens to a text on pollution.
sub_strands.links: The learner relates good listening skills to the learning of listening in Kiswahili.

outcomes.text: identify the main idea from a cause and effect text
pinpoint specific information from a cause and effect text

learning_experiences: predict events by focusing on the title and illustrations in a text,
individually, silently read a passage on pollution so as to internalize the information,
read the passage aloud in turns as they answer oral questions that are asked,
infer the meaning of given words using synonyms, contexts among others,
work with peers to recapture events in the text as they role play,
write answers to the questions given after the passage correctly.

Which skills should one use in order to read effectively?

sub_strands.pcis: Environmental education awareness: It is enhanced as the learner reads a passage on pollution.

infer meanings of words in a given text correctly

sub_strands.sub_strand: Word Classes: Primary Auxiliaries (Theme 3: Pollution)
learning_experiences: identify primary auxiliary verbs from a text,
search for the functions of primary auxiliary verbs from the internet or text books,
individually write down sentences using each of the primary auxiliary verbs identified,
collaborate to write a short paragraph on environmental conservation using primary auxiliary verbs,
read out the paragraphs to the rest of the class,
fill in blank spaces in sentences given using the correct form of the primary auxiliary verbs,
engage in a question and answer session using primary auxiliary verbs.
key_inquiry_questions: What are the functions of verbs in sentences?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Digital literacy: It is promoted as the learner uses digital devices to search for information from the internet.
Self-efficacy: It is affirmed as the learner’s confidence is boosted by using correct tenses in speech.
sub_strands.values: Respect: It is enhanced as the learner helps peers in constructing sentences correctly.
sub_strands.pcis: Environmental education awareness: It is enhanced as the learner writes a paragraph on environmental conservation.
sub_strands.links: The learner relates the concept of verbs to the learning of verbs in Kiswahili.

outcomes.text: identify primary auxiliary verbs in a text
use primary auxiliary verbs in sentences correctly
appreciate the importance of primary auxiliary verbs in communication

skills.name: Use the primary auxiliary verbs be, do and have
skills.mastery: Chooses the right form of be (is, are, was, were), do (do, does, did) and have (has, have, had) as a helping verb, makes it agree with the subject, and does not write she have finished or they was playing, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 7 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Grade 7 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Does not make has, have or do agree with the subject (she have finished, they has gone).

example.question: Wanjiru ___ finished her work.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "have" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: He, she and it take has; I, you, we and they take have.
misconceptions.feedback: Use has with he, she, it and one name (Wanjiru has). Use have with I, you, we and they.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses the wrong form of be (they was playing, I is ready).

example.question: The boys ___ playing football.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "was" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Many people or things take were or are.
misconceptions.feedback: Use was with I, he, she and it, and were with you, we, they and plural nouns: The boys were playing.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Puts did or does and then a past or -s verb (did went, does goes).

example.question: Otieno did not ___ to school.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "went" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: After did and does the main verb stays plain.
misconceptions.feedback: After do, does or did the main verb has no ending: Otieno did not go, he does not go.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

read a given poem and identify the structure,
recite and dramatize the given poem,
explain the words, phrases and sentences in a poem that help them to decipher the surface and deeper meaning,
relate the message of the poem to real life,
identify topics of poems such as pollution, list the topics down and display them in charts,
compose, type and share a poem related to pollution, with peers,
display their poems in a portfolio/chart/class noticeboard.

sub_strands.core_competences: Problem solving: It is enhanced as the learner attempts to solve simple problems while discussing the messages in a poem and relating them to real life.
sub_strands.values: Respect: It is enhanced as the learner respects diverse opinions while engaging in discussions and writing of poems on pollution.
sub_strands.pcis: Environmental conservation:It is developed as the learner composes poems on pollution.
sub_strands.links: The learner relates the study of poems to poetry in other learning areas such as Kiswahili and Creative arts and sports.

outcomes.text: identify the aspects of structure in a given poem
recognize the main ideas in a given poem

skills.name: Name the parts of a poem and the repetition in it
skills.mastery: Names the stanza (a group of lines), the line, the rhyme (matching end sounds), the rhythm (the beat) and the repetition (a word or line said again), and says the speaker of the poem is the persona, not always the poet, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 7 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Grade 7 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Mixes a stanza and a line of a poem.

example.question: What is a stanza?
example.correct_answer: A group of lines in a poem

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "One line of a poem" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A stanza is like a paragraph of lines.

skills.name: Tell gradable adjectives from non-gradable ones and use them correctly
skills.mastery: Uses very, quite and extremely with gradable adjectives (very tall, quite cold), uses absolutely and completely with non-gradable adjectives (absolutely perfect, completely empty), and does not write very perfect, more unique or very dead, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 7 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Uses very or more with a non-gradable adjective (very perfect, more unique, very dead).

example.question: The soup is ___ perfect.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "very" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Perfect, empty and dead cannot be more or less.
misconceptions.feedback: A non-gradable adjective such as perfect, empty, dead or unique cannot be graded, so use absolutely or completely, not very.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses absolutely or completely with a gradable adjective (absolutely tall, completely cold).

example.question: The boy is ___ tall for his age.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "absolutely" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Tall can be more or less. Very goes with it.
misconceptions.feedback: A gradable adjective such as tall, cold or big can be more or less, so use very, quite or extremely with it.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Makes a degree form of a non-gradable adjective (most unique, more empty, deader).

example.question: This painting is ___.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.

misconceptions.help: Unique means one of a kind, so it has no degrees.
misconceptions.feedback: Unique, perfect, empty and dead have no comparative or superlative form. Say unique, not more unique.

skills.name: Use adverbs of frequency and degree and put them in the right place
skills.mastery: Uses always, usually, often, sometimes and never for how often, and very, quite, too, almost and extremely for how much, puts a frequency adverb before the main verb and after be (she always arrives, he is never late), and does not write too for very, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 7 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Grade 7 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Puts the frequency adverb in the wrong place (She arrives always, he never is late).

example.question: Achieng ___ to school early.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "comes always" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Put the adverb before the main verb and after be.
misconceptions.feedback: A frequency adverb goes before the main verb (she always comes) and after be (he is never late).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses too where very is meant (too good, too beautiful).

example.question: The mandazi were ___ tasty, so we ate them all.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "too" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Too means more than is wanted. Very just adds strength.
misconceptions.feedback: Too means more than enough and is usually a problem (too hot to drink). Use very for a strong degree: very tasty.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses never with not (does not never come, I do not never go).

example.question: She ___ comes late.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "does not never" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Never already means not ever.
misconceptions.feedback: Never already makes the sentence negative, so do not add not: she never comes late.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Misspells a commonly misspelt word (seperate, definately, neccessary).

example.question: Please ___ the red beans from the green ones.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "seperate" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Look for the a in the middle: sep-a-rate.
misconceptions.feedback: Learn the tricky spellings: separate, definitely, necessary, occasion, accommodate, tomorrow. Look at the word, cover it, write it, check it.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes ei where ie is needed or the other way round (beleive, recieve).

example.question: We ___ a letter from Nairobi.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "recieve" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: I before e, except after c.
misconceptions.feedback: Write i before e except after c: believe, but receive and ceiling. A few words break the rule, such as seize and weird.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Doubles a letter that should not be doubled or leaves out a double letter (acommodate, occassion).

example.question: The hotel can ___ forty guests.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "acommodate" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Accommodate has two c and two m.
misconceptions.feedback: Accommodate has a double c and a double m. Occasion has a double c and one s.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Use indefinite and reflexive pronouns

Grade 7 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Writes hisself or theirselves for himself and themselves.

example.question: The boys taught ___ to swim.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "theirselves" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The reflexive pronouns end in -self or -selves.
misconceptions.feedback: The reflexive forms are myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves and themselves. There is no theirselves or hisself.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes ourself or yourselfs where the plural -selves is needed.

example.question: We made the cake ___.

misconceptions.reveals: Offer "ourself" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: We is many, so -selves.
misconceptions.feedback: Plural reflexive pronouns end in -selves: ourselves, yourselves, themselves.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Treats everyone, someone or nobody as plural (everyone are here, nobody are hurt).

example.question: Everyone ___ ready for the trip.

misconceptions.reveals: Offer "are" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Everyone is one word, so it is singular.

misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Use prepositions of position, time and place
skills.mastery: Chooses at, on or in for a time or a place (at 6 o'clock, on Monday, in June, at the gate, in the room) and under, above, beside, between, opposite, behind and in front of for position, and does not write at Monday or in the morning of Friday, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 7 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Uses the wrong preposition of time (at Monday, in 6 o'clock, on June).

example.question: The sports day is ___ Friday.

misconceptions.cause: Kiswahili influence (to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher)
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "in" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: On for days, in for months and years, at for clock times.
misconceptions.feedback: Use on with days (on Friday), in with months, years and parts of the day (in June, in the morning) and at with clock times (at 6 o'clock).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses beside for between, or between for many things (between the boys in the class).

example.question: The ball is ___ the two goal posts.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "beside" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Between is for two things.
misconceptions.feedback: Between is for two (or a few named) things and beside means next to: the ball is between the two posts.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses in for a point or a surface (in the gate, in the table).

example.question: Otieno waited ___ the school gate.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "in" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: At is for a point, on for a surface, in for inside.
misconceptions.feedback: Use at for a point (at the gate), on for a surface (on the table) and in for inside a space (in the room).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Use the conjunctions because, although, unless, until, while and so
skills.mastery: Chooses the conjunction for a reason (because), a contrast (although), a condition (unless), a limit in time (until), two things at once (while) and a result (so), and does not write although and but together or because and so together, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 7 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Uses although and but together (Although it rained, but we played).

example.question: ___ it was raining, we played football.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Although but" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Choose one of the two.
misconceptions.feedback: Although and but both show a contrast, so use only one of them: Although it was raining, we played.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses because and so together (Because he was late, so he ran).

example.question: Because Juma was late, ___ he ran to school.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "so" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: One joining word is enough.
misconceptions.feedback: Because and so both join a reason and a result. Use one: Because Juma was late, he ran. Or: Juma was late, so he ran.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses unless with a negative (unless you do not study).

example.question: You will fail ___ you study.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "unless you do not" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Unless already means if not.
misconceptions.feedback: Unless means if not, so do not add not: You will fail unless you study.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Picks a conjunction whose meaning does not fit (because for a contrast, unless for a reason).

example.question: ___ it was raining, we played football.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Because" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Ask what the two parts of the sentence say to each other: a reason, a contrast, a condition.
misconceptions.feedback: Choose the conjunction for the meaning: because for a reason, although for a contrast, unless for a condition, until for a limit in time, while for two things at once, so for a result.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.reveals: Offer "metaphor" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.

skills.name: Use this, that, these, those and quantifiers

misconceptions.error: Uses this with a plural noun or these with a singular noun (this books, these book).

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "This" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: This is one; these is many.

misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses this or these for something far away, or that or those for something near.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.

skills.name: Form adverbs from adjectives
skills.mastery: Adds -ly to most adjectives (quick, quickly), changes y to i before -ly (happy, happily), changes -le to -ly (gentle, gently), writes truly, and knows that the adverb of good is well and that fast and hard stay the same, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 7 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Grade 7 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Uses an adjective where the adverb is needed (she sings good, he ran quick, the baby smiled happy).

example.question: Wanjiru sings very ___.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "good" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Good describes a noun. Well describes a verb.
misconceptions.feedback: The adverb of good is well: she sings well. Good is an adjective: a good song.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Spells the -ly adverb wrongly (happyly, gentlely, truely).

example.question: The baby smiled ___.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "happyly" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: After a consonant, change y to i before -ly; -le becomes -ly; true becomes truly.
misconceptions.feedback: Change y to i before -ly (happily), change -le to -ly (gently) and write truly, not truely.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses hardly for hard or lately for late.

example.question: Otieno studied ___ for the test.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "hardly" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Hardly means almost not. The adverb of hard is hard.
misconceptions.feedback: Hard, fast and late are also adverbs without -ly. Hardly means almost not at all and lately means recently.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Use prefixes and suffixes and know what they do to a word
skills.mastery: Adds un-, dis-, re- and mis- to the front of a word (unhappy, disagree, replay, misunderstand) and -ful, -less, -ment and -ness to the end (careful, careless, enjoyment, kindness), says how the meaning changes, and keeps the spelling right (happy, happiness), in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 7 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Grade 7 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Uses the wrong prefix (unagree, disinteresting where uninteresting is meant).

example.question: The boys had a ___ about the rules.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "unagreement" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Dis- goes with agree, un- goes with happy.
misconceptions.feedback: Words take their own prefix: disagree, unhappy, replay, misunderstand. Check in a dictionary.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Gives the wrong meaning to a prefix or suffix (careless means full of care).

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "full of care" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The suffix -less means without.
misconceptions.feedback: The suffix -ful means full of and -less means without: careful is full of care, careless is without care.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Spells the new word wrongly when adding a suffix (happyness, beautifull).

misconceptions.help: Change y to i before the ending -ness.
misconceptions.feedback: When a word ends in consonant + y, change y to i before the suffix: happiness. The suffix -ful has one l: beautiful.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Give the meaning of common phrasal verbs and use them

prerequisites.reason: Grade 7 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Gives the wrong meaning of a phrasal verb (give up means present, run out of means run away).

example.question: The man gave up smoking. What did he do?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "He gave it to someone" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Read the whole sentence for the meaning.
misconceptions.feedback: A phrasal verb has its own meaning: give up means stop, look after means take care of, run out of means have no more.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses the wrong particle (look at the baby for look after, turn of the light).

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.

misconceptions.feedback: The particle changes the meaning: turn on starts a light, turn off stops it.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Reads a phrasal verb word by word (break down means break something).

misconceptions.help: Think what the whole phrase means.

skills.name: Join two simple sentences with a coordinating conjunction
skills.mastery: Joins two complete sentences with for, and, nor, but, or, yet or so and puts a comma before the conjunction, and does not join them with only a comma (a comma splice) or with no conjunction at all, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 7 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Grade 7 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Joins two sentences with only a comma (I was tired, I went to bed).

example.question: I was tired ___ I went to bed.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "," next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A comma alone cannot join two sentences.
misconceptions.feedback: Two complete sentences need a conjunction as well as the comma: I was tired, so I went to bed.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Leaves out the comma before the conjunction (She ran fast but she lost).

example.question: She ran fast___ but she lost.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Put a comma before the joining word.
misconceptions.feedback: A comma goes before for, and, nor, but, or, yet or so when it joins two sentences: She ran fast, but she lost.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Chooses a conjunction that does not fit (It rained, and we stayed home when we wanted to go).

example.question: It was raining, ___ we stayed indoors.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "but" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Think: does the second part show a result, a contrast or an addition?
misconceptions.feedback: Pick the conjunction for the meaning: so for a result, but and yet for a contrast, and for an addition, or for a choice.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Tell personification and flashback in a story

Grade 7 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Calls a plain description personification, or misses personification.

example.question: Which sentence has personification?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The wind was strong." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Does a thing act like a person?
misconceptions.feedback: Personification gives a thing or an animal a human action or feeling: the wind whispered.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Says a flashback jumps forward in time.

example.question: What is a flashback?
example.wrong_answer: A jump to the future of the story
example.correct_answer: A return to an earlier time in the story

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A jump to the future of the story" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Flash back means go back.
misconceptions.feedback: A flashback takes the reader back to something that happened earlier.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Calls a simile personification.

example.question: Which sentence has personification?
example.wrong_answer: The cloud was like a pillow.
example.correct_answer: The cloud smiled at the hills.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The cloud was like a pillow." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A simile compares with like or as. Personification gives human actions.
misconceptions.feedback: Personification gives a human action to a thing (the cloud smiled). A simile uses like or as (the cloud was like a pillow).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Tell the silent consonant letters in words

misconceptions.error: Picks a sounded letter as the silent one (in knife, says f).

misconceptions.error: Picks the wrong silent letter in a word (castle: c, honest: n).

misconceptions.error: Calls an active sentence passive, or the other way round.

misconceptions.error: Gives a positive tag after a positive sentence (You are coming, are you).

example.question: You are coming, ___?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "are you" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A positive sentence takes a negative tag.
misconceptions.feedback: A positive sentence takes a negative tag (You are coming, aren't you) and a negative sentence takes a positive tag (You are not coming, are you).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses isn't it for every tag (They are late, isn't it).

example.question: They are late, ___?

misconceptions.cause: Copied from the usual spoken Kenyan English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "isn't it" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The tag repeats the helping verb and the subject.
misconceptions.feedback: The tag repeats the helping verb and the subject as a pronoun: They are late, aren't they. Isn't it is not for every tag.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses the wrong helping verb in the tag (She likes tea, isn't she).

example.question: She likes tea, ___?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "isn't she" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Use the helping verb of the sentence: likes needs does.
misconceptions.feedback: The tag uses the helping verb that fits the sentence: She likes tea, doesn't she. For present simple, use do or does.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Poems (Theme 15: Tourist attraction sites: africa)
learning_experiences: recite and dramatize the given poems for enjoyment in groups,
outline the subject matter and share with peers,
identify the messages conveyed in the poems and make notes,
highlight lessons learnt from the poems and discuss the lessons brought out through the relationship between characters in the poem,
present them in posters to be displayed in the notice boards for peer review.
key_inquiry_questions: Which lessons have you learnt from poems before?
How can you say what is in the poem in your own words?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Problem solving: It is enhanced as the learner gets ideas from poems on how to solve problems of self and others.
Self-efficacy: It is enhanced as the learner focuses on achieving set tasks while reciting and dramatising poems.
sub_strands.values: Respect: It is enriched as the learner provides feedback on lessons identified by peers with dignity.
sub_strands.pcis: Social cohesion: It is nurtured as the learner appreciates the role of their peers as they recite and dramatise the poems.
sub_strands.links: The skills acquired by learners as they dramatise poems and other genres are related to performance techniques in Creative arts and sports.

outcomes.text: identify the ideas in the Poems
derive the lessons learnt in the poem
recognise the role of poems in addressing societal issues

sub_strands.sub_strand: Functional Writing: Personal Journals (Theme 15: Tourist attraction sites: africa)
learning_experiences: explain the purpose of keeping a diary or journal,
view sample journals and identify the components,
in groups, brainstorm and choose ideas to write about using prompts like: - what was your experience during the visit to the national park?
bring to school a physical journal or sign-up for an online journal or improvise one and make entries,
reflect on an experience, and record thoughts and feelings about it and enter them in the journal,
re-read the entries and add additional thoughts,
publish the journals they have created through posters and social media.
key_inquiry_questions: Why do we write journals?
What would you like to remember about an experience?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Self efficacy: It is promoted as the learner engages in self-driven tasks as they practise writing journals.
Communication and collaboration: It is enhanced as the learner makes suggestions on improvements to be made while brainstorming on journal entries in groups.
sub_strands.values: Love: It is inculcated as the learner jointly reviews journals written by peers with compassion.
sub_strands.pcis:
Creative thinking skills: They are enhanced as the learner generates experiences to record in the journals
Citizenship education: It is brought out as the learner talks about a visit to a national park
sub_strands.links: Journaling is a skill that relates to formative assessment in all subjects including Agriculture .

outcomes.text: outline the components of a personal journal
create a personal journal on varied experiences
evaluate a journal for correctness and relevance

indicators.indicator: Ability to write, perform songs and poems using relevant features of performance

levels.ME: The learner writes, performs songs and poems using relevant features

levels.BE: The learner writes, performs song and poems which are only known to them and only uses selected features which they know.

levels.BE: The learner delivers speeches, oral reports with many inconsistencies
